name: death coach
sources: Evans-Wentz, W. Y. The Fairy-Faith in Celtic Countries. Gerrards Cross: Colin Smythe Humanities Press, 1911, 221.
Westropp, T. J. Folklore of Clare: A Folklore Survey of Country Clare and County Clare Folk-Tales and Myths. Ennis, Co. Clare: Clasp Press, 2000, 10-12.
Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: The death coach is an Irish folkloric object sent from the land of the dead. On foggy nights a black coach could draw up to a home. Black horses pulled it, and it carried no coachman or passengers. Its driver, if present, had no head. The horses could be headless as well. The coach came to collect a person from this life. It never left the earth empty. A person who was not scheduled to die became the victim if he stood in its path. People were told to avoid it and never to stop it from taking its intended passenger. A sighting of the death coach foretold death, just as the cry of the Banshee did.

okr.objective: Records the death coach as a supernatural omen of death in Irish folklore.
key_results: The death coach was an Irish black coach drawn by headless horses on foggy nights.
It came from the land of the dead to collect a scheduled victim.
Anyone who stood in its path became the victim in place of that person.
A sighting of the death coach foretold death, as did the Banshee's cry.
evidence: Evans-Wentz, The Fairy-Faith in Celtic Countries, 1911, p. 221
